words.definition: Relating to a community or its residents and their shared public duties.
words.example: She felt a strong civic duty to vote in every local election.
words.mnemonic: Think of a Honda Civic, the car everyone in the city seems to drive — civic is about the city and its people.

words.definition: Shared by all members of a group rather than owned by one person.
words.example: The tenants cooked their meals in a communal kitchen at the end of the hall.
words.mnemonic: Hidden inside is 'commune' — a place where everyone shares everything.

words.definition: Done or shared by all members of a group acting together.
words.example: The factory workers reached a collective decision to strike.
words.mnemonic: Collect + ive — you collect everyone together into one unit.

words.definition: Unity and mutual support among people who share a cause.
words.example: The strikers stood in solidarity, refusing to cross the picket line.
words.mnemonic: Hear 'solid' — a group standing rock-solid behind one another.

words.definition: The quality of sticking together to form a united whole.
words.example: Years of playing together gave the team a cohesion no rival could match.
words.mnemonic: Co + adhesion — parts that adhere and stick as one.

words.definition: A brotherhood or association of people sharing a common interest or profession.
words.example: He joined a college fraternity and moved in with his new brothers.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'frater' means brother, so it is a band of brothers.

words.definition: A warm feeling of trust and friendship among companions.
words.example: The soldiers shared a deep camaraderie forged during long months at war.
words.mnemonic: Hear 'comrade' inside — comrades are the ones who share it.

words.definition: A friendly bond among people who share interests or good company.
words.example: After the service, the congregation lingered for food and fellowship.
words.mnemonic: A ship full of fellows sailing together — picture the Fellowship of the Ring.

words.definition: Believing that everyone deserves the same rights and status.
words.example: Their egalitarian household split every chore evenly between the partners.
words.mnemonic: French 'égal' means equal — this outlook wants everyone égal.

words.definition: A system that ranks people or things by status or authority.
words.example: In the company hierarchy, interns answered to managers who answered to directors.
words.mnemonic: Say it as 'higher-archy' — it's all about who sits higher up.

words.definition: To arrange people or things into separate ranked layers.
words.example: Extreme wealth gaps tend to stratify a society into rich and poor worlds.
words.mnemonic: 'Strata' are the layers of rock geologists study — to make layers.

words.definition: To push a person or group aside and treat them as unimportant.
words.example: The new policy marginalized older workers who lacked computer skills.
words.mnemonic: Shoved out to the margin — the blank edge of the page where nothing matters.

words.definition: To deliberately exclude someone from a group or from society.
words.example: After he was caught cheating, his teammates ostracized him for the rest of the season.
words.mnemonic: Ancient Greeks scratched names on 'ostraca' (pottery shards) to vote a person out.

words.definition: To make someone feel unwelcome or turn them against you.
words.example: His constant criticism alienated the very friends he most needed.
words.mnemonic: Make someone feel like an alien — a stranger who does not belong.

words.definition: To absorb people or ideas fully into a larger group or culture.
words.example: Newcomers often work hard to assimilate into their adopted country's customs.
words.mnemonic: Hear 'similar' — you become similar to the group around you.

words.definition: To separate or set apart one group from others, often by race or class.
words.example: For decades the city tried to segregate its schools by neighborhood, keeping children apart by race.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'separate gate' — a gate built to keep groups apart.

words.definition: The practice of making sure everyone is welcomed and actively involved.
words.example: The new hiring policy emphasized inclusion, opening doors to candidates of every background.
words.mnemonic: Starts with 'in' — it's about bringing people IN, never leaving them out.

words.definition: To strip a person or group of the legal right to vote.
words.example: Poll taxes were designed to disenfranchise poor voters who couldn't afford to pay them.
words.mnemonic: 'Dis-' (remove) + 'franchise' (your vote) = your vote gets taken away.

words.definition: To grant someone the legal right to vote or the full rights of citizenship.
words.example: The 1920 amendment finally enfranchised women, letting them cast ballots for the first time.
words.mnemonic: Break it down: en- (to make) + franchise. A 'franchise' is the right to vote, so to enfranchise is to give someone that franchise.

words.definition: The whole body of people who legally belong to a nation or place.
words.example: The mayor urged the entire citizenry to turn out and vote on Tuesday.
words.mnemonic: 'Citizen' + '-ry' (a collective, like 'peasantry') = all the citizens together.

words.definition: The ordinary people living in a particular country or area.
words.example: News of the tax hike angered the populace, and crowds soon filled the streets.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'populate' — the people who populate a place.

words.definition: A specific segment of a population sharing traits like age or income.
words.example: Advertisers targeted a young, urban demographic with the new streaming service.
words.mnemonic: 'Demo-' (Greek for people) + '-graphic' (measuring) = a measured slice of people.

words.definition: The group of voters represented by an elected official.
words.example: The senator flew home to hear concerns from her constituency before the big vote.
words.mnemonic: Shares its root with 'constitute' — the voters who constitute a district.

words.definition: A small, often self-interested group within a larger organization or party.
words.example: A rebel faction broke away from the main party over the terms of the peace deal.
words.mnemonic: Hides 'fract-' as in 'fracture' — a piece fractured off from the whole.

words.definition: A temporary union of groups or parties for combined action.
words.example: Three small parties formed a coalition to build a governing majority.
words.mnemonic: Like separate lumps of 'coal' brought together into one fire — groups uniting.

words.definition: A formal agreement between nations or groups to cooperate and support each other.
words.example: The two nations signed an alliance to defend one another if either was attacked.
words.mnemonic: Contains 'ally' — allies bound together by a pact.

words.definition: An official connection or membership with a group or organization.
words.example: She listed her affiliation with the local chess club on the application form.
words.mnemonic: Hear 'a-FILE-iation' — you get filed under a group you belong to.

words.definition: Loyalty or commitment owed to a leader, country, or cause.
words.example: The soldiers swore allegiance to the crown before marching off to war.
words.mnemonic: Hear 'a-LIEGE-ance' — a liege is the lord you stay loyal to.

words.definition: Strong disagreement with an officially held opinion or decision.
words.example: A single justice voiced dissent, arguing the majority's ruling was deeply unjust.
words.mnemonic: 'Dis-' (apart) + 'sent' (to feel, as in sentiment) = feeling differently from the rest.

words.definition: A person who publicly opposes the policies of their government.
words.example: The dissident was jailed for essays that mocked the regime and its leaders.
words.mnemonic: From 'dis-' + 'sedere' (to sit) — one who 'sits apart' from official views.

words.definition: Behavior that matches a group's accepted rules, standards, or expectations.
words.example: The strict dress code enforced a dull conformity, with every student looking identical.
words.mnemonic: Conform + -ity: to 'form with' the group — shaping yourself to match everyone around you.

words.definition: A person who refuses to follow society's usual customs, beliefs, or expected behavior.
words.example: While the others wore suits, she showed up in paint-stained overalls, a proud nonconformist.
words.mnemonic: Non + conformist: NOT one who forms with the crowd — the person who won't fit the mold.

words.definition: Someone who rises in armed opposition against an established government or authority.
words.example: The insurgents seized the radio station and broadcast their demands to the capital.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'in-surge' — a surge of fighters rising up against the rulers.

words.definition: Trying to secretly weaken or overthrow an established system, government, or institution.
words.example: The pamphlets were banned as subversive, since they quietly urged workers to disobey the regime.
words.mnemonic: Sub (under) + verse (turn): turning things over from underneath, secretly.

words.definition: A violent, organized attempt by many people to overthrow their rulers.
words.example: The failed insurrection ended with tanks in the square and its leaders in prison.
words.mnemonic: In-sur-RECT-ion: people 'surrect' (like resurrect, to rise) against the state.

words.definition: A popular act of resistance or rebellion against a government or authority.
words.example: News of the tax spread quickly, and by dawn a full uprising had gripped three provinces.
words.mnemonic: Picture people literally 'up-rising' from their seats to fight the king.

words.definition: To rebel violently against those in power.
words.example: When wages were cut again, the miners finally revolted and stormed the company office.
words.mnemonic: Re-VOLT: an electric jolt of anger that makes people turn against their leaders.

words.definition: To organize and prepare a group of people or resources for action.
words.example: Within hours the organizers mobilized thousands of volunteers to sandbag the flooding riverbank.
words.mnemonic: Mobile + -ize: make a crowd mobile — get them moving into action.

words.definition: To stir up strong public feeling, usually for or against a cause.
words.example: For years she agitated for prison reform, giving speeches until lawmakers finally listened.
words.mnemonic: Like an agitator in a washing machine, stirring everything up violently.

words.definition: A state of angry dissatisfaction that often leads to protests or disturbances.
words.example: Rising food prices sparked weeks of unrest, with crowds blocking roads across the city.
words.mnemonic: Un + rest: no rest — a society too troubled to sit still.

words.definition: To make something better by changing or correcting its faults.
words.example: The new mayor promised to reform the crumbling school system within her first term.
words.mnemonic: Re-form: 'form again' — reshape something broken into a better shape.

words.definition: Favoring social improvement and new ideas rather than tradition.
words.example: Her progressive policies on childcare and clean energy attracted younger voters.
words.mnemonic: Progress-ive: always pushing forward toward progress and new ideas.

words.definition: Supporting extreme or fundamental change, especially in politics.
words.example: His radical plan would scrap the entire tax code and start over from scratch.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'radix' = root; radical change goes down to the very root.

words.definition: A system of ideas and beliefs that guides a group's politics or economics.
words.example: The two parties clashed less over facts than over their opposing ideologies.
words.mnemonic: Idea + -ology: the 'study or system of ideas' a group holds.

words.definition: A set of guiding beliefs or principles that someone lives by.
words.example: "Leave every campsite cleaner than you found it" was the old ranger's lifelong credo.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'credo' = 'I believe' (same root as 'creed').

words.definition: The guiding spirit and shared values that define a community or group.
words.example: The startup's ethos of 'move fast, share credit' shaped every meeting.
words.mnemonic: Ethos sounds like 'ethics' — both from Greek; picture a group's shared ethics-spirit.

words.definition: The essential moral rules and accepted behaviors of a particular society.
words.example: Loud haggling was fine at the bazaar but violated the mores of the quiet gallery.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'mos/mores' gives us 'morals' — mores are a group's shared morals.

words.definition: A standard or typical pattern of behavior expected within a group.
words.example: Working from home became the norm after the downtown office closed.
words.mnemonic: A carpenter's 'norma' was a right-angle square — the standard everything is measured against.

words.definition: A widely accepted practice or unspoken agreement that most people follow.
words.example: By convention, the host sits at the head of the table.
words.mnemonic: People CONVENE (come together) and settle on a shared way — a convention.

words.definition: A traditional, repeated way of doing something within a culture.
words.example: It is their custom to remove shoes before entering the house.
words.mnemonic: A 'customer' returns out of habit — a custom is a habitual practice of a people.

words.definition: A belief or practice passed down through generations over time.
words.example: Lighting candles on the last night of the year is a family tradition.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'tradere' means to hand over — tradition is handed down through the ages.

words.definition: An established organization or long-standing practice within a society.
words.example: Marriage is one of the oldest institutions in human history.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'statuere', to set up (like a 'statue') — firmly set in place.

words.definition: A system of administration run by many officials following rigid rules.
words.example: Getting the permit meant weeks lost in bureaucracy and endless paperwork.
words.mnemonic: 'Bureau' (desk) + '-cracy' (rule) = rule by desks and paperwork.

words.definition: The process and manner of controlling and directing an organization or state.
words.example: Poor governance left the company with no clear way to make decisions.
words.mnemonic: Greek 'kybernan' means to steer a ship — a governor steers the organization.

words.definition: The right or ability to govern oneself and make independent decisions.
words.example: The region was granted autonomy and now sets its own laws.
words.mnemonic: 'auto' (self) + 'nomos' (law) = making your own laws; self-rule.

words.definition: The supreme power and full authority of a state to rule itself.
words.example: The nation defended its sovereignty against foreign interference in its elections.
words.mnemonic: A sovereign sits above all (think 'super') — sovereignty is that supreme power.

words.definition: The official power to make legal decisions within a defined area or scope.
words.example: The local police had no jurisdiction over crimes committed across the state line.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'juris' (law) + 'diction' (speaking) = the power to speak the law.

words.definition: An official order or granted authority to carry out a specific policy.
words.example: Winning by a landslide gave the president a clear mandate for reform.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'manus' (hand) + 'dare' (give) = handed the authority to act.

words.definition: An official order issued by a ruler that carries the force of law.
words.example: By royal decree, the harvest festival was declared a public holiday.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'decernere', to decide — a decree is a ruler's decided command handed down.

words.definition: A formal command or public proclamation issued by an authority.
words.example: The emperor's edict banned all trade with the rival kingdom.
words.mnemonic: 'e' (out) + 'dict' (speak, as in dictate) = a command spoken out to everyone.

words.definition: A formal written rule made and enforced by the governing body of a country or state.
words.example: A new statute now requires every landlord to install smoke alarms in each bedroom.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'stat' (immediately) — a written rule carved on a statue's base that you must obey stat.
